utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who do I call, do I call Mr. Whiting or Ms. Richterova? Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, I'm calling the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. Yes, Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness, can you please state your full name and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Josip Josipovic, born on the 15th of February, 1967, in Hrvatska Dubica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You are of Croatian nationality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You served your compulsory military service between March 1989 and March 1990?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And until 1991, you were switchman at the railway station?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You mentioned that you were born in Hrvatska Dubica. Which town or which village in Dubica area did you live?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Predore village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Predore village, is it part of some other bigger village?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: It's eight kilometres away from Hrvatska Dubica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Talking about Predore, is it a Croat or a Serb village?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: It had a mixed population; Croats, Serbs and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How many people lived, approximately, in your village?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Not many. There were perhaps 15 houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And how many of them belonged to Croats?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Five or six.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: To Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Around the same number.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you tell us what other villages were there in the area of Dubica?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Donji Cerovljani, Bacin, Sanac, Visnjica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Which of these villages you must mentioned belonged to Croats?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: All of them were Croat. In fact, all the villages had a mixed population, almost all of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was there any village with predominantly Serb population?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Zivaja.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honours, just -- I forgot to mention where you could find the village of Hrvatska Dubica. It's in the atlas on the page 21, grid D3. Your Honours will see somewhere in the middle a town called Bosanska Dubica, and right above it is the place called Dubica, which is Hrvatska Dubica. It means that it is on the territory of Croatia. Bosanska Dubica is on the territory of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you very briefly describe the relationship between Croats and Serbs until 1990 in the area of Dubica?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: We lived normally, having no inkling of what would happen later. Everything worked well in our human relations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did there come a time when the situation changed?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The situation changed later. When Tito died, Yugoslavia was supposed to get a new president. Two or three presidents, in fact, changed before the end -- before the beginning of the war when Croatia wanted to separate from the rest of Yugoslavia. However, it caused the outbreak of a war.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What -- what caused the outbreak of the war?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Croatia wanted to be independent. Croatian wanted to have its own government, and Serbs rebelled against that. They wanted a Greater Serbia. In fact, at one stage they wanted Greater Serbia, and at another point they wanted to stay in the former Yugoslavia, and that caused a quarrel, and it caused the system to break down.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know whether Croatia formed their own armed forces? And I am referring to 1990.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Croatia held its elections, and after the elections it established its own Croatian police and the Croatian army that was called ZNG, the Home Guards Corps. When that happened, those Serbs who worked on the police force in the times of Yugoslavia rebelled. They used to wear different emblems, Yugoslav emblems like the five-pointed star, and they were very much against the introduction of the Croatian chequer-board standard flag.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I please interrupt? In the answer to the previous question, did the witness not say in fact at one stage they wanted Greater Serbia, and at another point they wanted to stay in the former -- Croatia. I see it says the former Yugoslavia. I'm not quite sure whether the witness said Croatia or the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you please clarify to the Judge whether they meant that they wanted to stay in former Yugoslavia or whether they wanted to stay in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: They wanted to remain part of Yugoslavia, and they wanted Croatia as a whole to remain part of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I now understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What happened to these Serbs who didn't want to wear the chequer-board sign?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: The Serbs who didn't want to wear the chequer-board emblem stood down from their posts in the police force of Croatia and became renegades. They created their own units purportedly for the defence of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Let's now talk about the area of Dubica, and tell us, were there any ZNG units in 1990 or 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, just after the elections. The new Croatian police and the Home Guards Corps were immediately established.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When -- when we are talking about these Home Guards Corps, are you referring to ZNG?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Where is -- ZNG, where were they located? Where was their headquarters?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: The headquarters was in Hrvatska Dubica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Up until 1991, do you know of their strength in -- in the Dubica area?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand the question. You mean Croatian units, the police, or the army, or the total?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm referring now to ZNG. Do you know how many men approximately were member of ZNG in the area of Dubica?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Just a few. A couple of Croatian villages only joined the Home Guards Corps and the police. Let me try to give you a number. Perhaps a hundred men all in all.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What about Serbs? Did -- did they form some armed units as well?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They formed their own units wishing to stay within the former Yugoslavia, and they called them TO, Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Where was their headquarter? I'm talking about this Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Their headquarters was in Dubica hills, Dubicka Brda, overlooking Hrvatska Dubica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What about police? You already talk about Croatian police. Was there any Serb police?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, after the Croatian police and troops withdrew from Hrvatska Dubica, the Serbs had their own police force there and their TO.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We will talk about this little bit later, but when was it that Croatian police and troop -- troops withdrew from Hrvatska Dubica?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: The 13th or the 14th September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Let's talk now about ZNG and TO. What kind -- did you join ZNG?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What were the circumstances you joined ZNG?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I was not able to go to work and I couldn't keep my job, so I had no choice by to join the ZNG, and that was in July, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Which we are?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What kinds of weapons ZNG -- did ZNG have at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: ZNG had hunting weapons at the time and some museum rifles. Whatever they could lay their hands on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What about the Serb forces which were in the area? How were they armed?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Serb forces had the support of the former Yugoslav People's Army, and the Yugoslav People's Army supplied them with automatic and other weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you ever see -- you say that JNA supplied them with weapons. Did you ever see that JNA, any unit of JNA would provide or deliver these weapons?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I did. When I was coming from Hrvatska Dubica to my own village, Predore, helicopters were hovering over the village, and once when I was going into Predore to visit my parents, I saw a JNA helicopter hovering first over the village and then moving 500 metres away, perhaps, where it landed on the road, and those renegade Serbs were waiting there. And then they proceeded to unload weapons from the helicopter and put them into trucks and some other passenger vehicles that they had seized earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you still remember which directions did they take these weapons, or this truck drove which direction?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Towards Zivaja, which was a Serb-populated village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You -- you also mention "those renegade Serbs." Who are you referring to? Who were they? Which unit did they belong?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't really know to which unit they belonged. They wore a variety of insignia, including the five-pointed star and emblems with the inscription "SAO Krajina." They wore cockades. You couldn't tell any more who was who and how they were -- who they were supposed to be. They were TO, the police, local defence. We referred to them as Serbs or Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to show you three patches and ask you whether you would be able to recognise any of these patches, whether any of them was -- you could see wearing people -- Serb people in Dubica. The first one is Exhibit 266, and I would provide hard copy, because it usually takes a little bit of time to display it on the screen. So if we could place it on the ELMO. Can you please have a look at this patch and tell us whether you ever seen this patch on any uniforms in Dubica? It's right next to you.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw this one worn on camouflage uniforms and the olive-grey uniforms alike.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know who wore these -- who wore this -- this patch?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: The police of the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We will talk about police Krajina little bit later. Now I would like to show you another patch. It is -- it is 65 ter number 641, and I will again provide a hard copy. We manage to display it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we first see the number of this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you have a look at this patch and tell us whether you saw this patch on any uniforms in Dubica?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Who -- who wore these patches?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Serb army and the Serb police, the special purpose police. I don't know what they called themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This one, not the previous one?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The previous one has already been tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Has it. Okay. This document with number 01187435 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be exhibit number 288, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And there is a last one. Its number is -- 65 ter number is 640, and ERN is 01187450. Witness, did you see the similar sign or the same sign like this in the patch in Dubica?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did see it in Dubica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness, this one says down below "Ugljevik."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where is "Ugljevik"?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It is in Cyrillic. It is down below.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you please show the Judges where the word "Ugljevik" is written on that document, please.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did people who you saw wearing this patch, did they have also the sign of Ugljevik or was there something else?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember whether it said something else or whether it said "Ugljevik," but I do remember this patch very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What does "Ugljevik" mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know what "Ugljevik" means?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Ugljevik is a town in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is the witness able to tell us what the other writing means or what the writing -- the rest of the writing says?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Would you be so kind and tell the Judges what we can see in writing on this patch.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: It says, "Special Police Units," "Blue," and then "Ugljevik."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is "blue" also on this writing?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It is this word "Plavi."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You stated that you saw this patch on uniforms in -- in Dubica. Which unit or which forces wore these patches?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: These patches were worn by men who came from Bosna to help when they were attacking Jasenovac, and then Lipan [phoen], Pakrac.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And these people from Bosnia who came to help, what ethnicity did they were?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: They were of Serbian ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document with ERN number 01187450 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 289, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm -- I'm done with these. It can be removed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You mentioned that JNA supplied Serb -- Serbs with weapons, and you describe how they delivered weapons in this helicopter. Did -- did you see only one helicopter or were there more than one helicopters you saw in Dubica area?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: There were several of them, and on a number of occasions this helicopter flew over, and that was something that happened before I'd joined the ZNG.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And after you joined ZNG, were you aware whether the supply of weapons continue?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How did you know it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I knew because I was in Hrvatska Dubica. I left Hrvatska Dubica to visit my parents in their village, and my mother told me that the helicopter had landed again, and on one occasion when I went there my mother told me the same again, and I went and saw it for myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You mention JNA helicopters. Did you also see JNA forces? Did you see JNA soldiers in -- in Dubica area?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it would be difficult to say JNA soldiers. They wore all sort of insignia, so it's difficult to say whether it was a TO soldier or member of the special police or of the Krajina police or whether it was a Chetnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What do you mean that it was difficult to -- to distinguish? Can you be more specific? You cannot say whether someone was a JNA soldier or whether someone was a TO member or that someone was a policeman?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was difficult to distinguish them. All we knew is that they were fighting for the same objective, a Greater Serbia and in order to preserve Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What was the role of ZNG in Dubica? You were a member of ZNG. What was the role?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: To exercise authority, to implement the law, to enforce the law. ZNG was there at the time of the former Yugoslavia. And what the TO was was also the ZNG at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How would you describe what was happening in summer of 1991 in Dubica? Were there any clashes? What was happening in summertime of 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: In the summer of 1991, the police was carrying out its duties, and the ZNG was helping the police at the time. The Serbs who lived in that area, in Hrvatska Dubica, were creating hatred amongst themselves, and they were scaring each other by referring to the ZNG and the Croatian police, and at such times they would cross the River Una at night, and they would go to Bosanska Dubica. The JNA was present in Bosanska Dubica, and naturally they reported to the JNA and gave them false information as to the situation in Dubica. They spread hatred in this way and made the JNA hate the Croats; the Croatian police and the Croatian army. Naturally, the JNA provided them with weapons. This all happened at night because they were afraid to sleep in Hrvatska Dubica and in their villages, so they went to Bosna. That's where they got the weapons, and then they would open fire at night. They would open fire over the Una. They would open fire on the Croatian troops, and they would fire at Croatian houses. At night they would return as if nothing had happened.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to speak up or to approach the microphone as the interpreter is having difficulty hearing him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness, would you be so kind and lean against the microphone a -- closer to microphone because the interpreters cannot hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And also speak loud, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You said that these Serbs left for Bosanska Dubica, to stay there overnight. Did they always return in the morning?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they would always return in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What was your task? You were a member of ZNG. What did -- you specifically, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the ZNG at the very beginning. At the very beginning I was issued with a sniper rifle, and I was assigned to patrol a bridge, to be present at a bridge, at the border between Hrvatska and Bosanska Dubica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now, how long did you have this sniper rifle? How long did you hold this assignment?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: For a brief period of time. I had that rifle, as I said, and on one occasion shooting broke out, and at the time someone ordered me to return fire. I don't know who issued this order, but I refused to comply with the order. I didn't want to open fire. I was a sniper in the former JNA. I know what my duty is. I know what I'm supposed to do. And now I was no longer a desirable individual, and my sniper rifle was taken away from me and given to someone else.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And after that, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: After that, I received an M-48 rifle which I carried around with me. I was in a state of readiness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were you involved -- after this, were you involved in any attacks on Serb forces, or did you stay in the town?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I stayed on in town.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were you able to go back to your village to visit your parents?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was difficult. I had to go there at night to reach my village, and then I could visit my home and stay at my home during the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You stated no, but then you said it was difficult, you had to go overnight. So did you go or you -- you didn't go?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How often did you go home?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how many times I went home throughout that entire period while I was a member of the ZNG in Hrvatska Dubica. Perhaps I went there between eight and 10 times.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You already mentioned that at some point in September ZNG and Croatian police left Hrvatska Dubica. At the time when they left, where were you? Were you in Dubica or at home in Predore?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I was at home in Predore.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know why ZNG and why Croatian forces left Hrvatska Dubica?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The JNA launched an attack, as well as the rebellious Serbs we have already mentioned. They launched an attack, and they wanted to put Hrvatska Dubica under their control as well as the surrounding places and villages. At that point, the Croatian police, the ZNG, and the population withdrew.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When you say population withdrew as well, are you talking about civilian population of Croat ethnicity or Serb ethnicity or both ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm referring to those of Croatian nationality, but there were several Serbs and Muslims who also fled before the JNA and the rebellious Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When -- when you -- you keep repeating the "rebellious Serbs." So Dubica was attacked by JNA, and which other forces were together with JNA?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the Serbian forces were there, Serbian forces who were fighting for the SAO Krajina. I don't really know what their objective was though.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now, you -- you said that at the time when ZNG and Croatian forces left Dubica you were in your village Predore. What happened in Predore? How did you -- first, how did you learn that civilians left Dubica?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I heard about that because I was in Novska at one point in time. I returned home, and upon returning I saw a -- people I knew who were playing at war. I asked them what they were doing, and they said what the situation was like. They said that the JNA and rebellious Serbs had launched an attack and that they had to withdraw, that the Croatian army and police had to withdraw, as well as the population. They said that the -- they had to ensure that the civilian population could withdraw. I entered my village where my mother lived, and we got ready to flee, naturally. Once we had packed everything, the Serbs came from all sides. They encircled the village, and they then imprisoned us and --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'll stop you here --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: -- assembled you all together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just get clarification? What is meant by "people playing at war"?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask, Your Honour, the same question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you please explain what do you mean by they were "playing at war"?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: There was some sort of a -- a train with some carriages in which there were rocks, and there was a diesel machine behind those carriages which was moving the carriages, and there were mortars, handmade mortars on those -- in the carriages that had been made by amateur workers in the ironworks. These mortars didn't have site-setters, didn't have devises to measure the distance. Two idiots would have to use such mortars. One would have to hold onto it and the other would have to put the shell in the device.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Why did they bring this train with mortars?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And who are the "they"?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: First, who brought this train, and why did they bring this train?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: As I have already said, that train arrived so that the Croatian population could withdraw. It was in the possession of the Croatian army, the ZNG.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And were they able to use these mortars?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, of course. But no one knew where the shell would fall or whether the shell would explode.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now I would like to return to your village. When you said that Serbs arrive from four sides, who were these Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They came from all sides. They were members of the JNA, of the Territorial Defence, the police of SAO Krajina. They were Chetniks, people fighting for a Greater Serbia. I don't really know who they were. They had all sorts of insignia on them. Anyone who got hold of insignia of any kind would -- would wear such insignia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you know anybody from these people? Did you know anybody by name?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did know about perhaps a dozen men by name.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you tell us who you knew by name?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Paukovic, Rajko; Paukovic, Dubravko; Mico Tepic; Djordje Ratkovic; Djuro Jerinic; Branko Kotur, and others. I can't remember any other names.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know a person by name Veljko Radjunovic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. There was a Zeljko [as interpreted] and Stevo Radjunovic. And Momcilo Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, did you say Zeljko or Veljko?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Veljko. Veljko.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know who Veljko Radjunovic and Stevo Radjunovic were?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Stevo Radjunovic, he was the most important person in the police, in the TO, in the JNA, and within the Chetnik command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What about Veljko Radjunovic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Veljko Radjunovic, Stevo's father, was sort of an advisor to him and to Momcilo Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And who was Momcilo Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Momcilo Kovacevic and Stevo had a lot of influence in the Croatian army. I don't know whether Stevo was the main person or Momcilo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, did you say that Momcilo Kovacevic and Stevo had lots of influence in Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: No. They weren't in the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So what -- what kind of army? It was probably some mistake. What kind of army? Was it Croatian or Serb army or Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: We're talking about the Serbian army, the Serbian police, the Serbian Territorial Defence, the Serbian population.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And these three men, were they also present when these Serbs arrived to your village?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: After they arrived to your village what happened? What did they do?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: They gathered the people in one place. They separated six or seven of us from the others. There was one slightly younger person. They created a live shield, and they forced us to head down to the Sava River so that they could reconnoiter the area and check out the situation to see what Croatia had at its disposal, how many troops they had, what the strength of the police force was, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And after that where did they take you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: After that, they returned us to the village, and then they took us from the village to Hrvatska Dubica or, rather, to Dubicka Brda where they had their command. And they had a headquarters there for mortars, howitzers, tanks, cannons, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When you say, "They took us to Dubicka Brda," how many of you were taken to Dubicka Brda?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Two of us. My nephew and I.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What is the name of your nephew?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mico Coric.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Just one clarification. You said they had a headquarters there. Who -- who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we're talking about Serbs again, the Serb army, and in that Serb army there was, of course, the TO. Anyway, I was just referring to Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How long -- how long did you stay in this headquarter in Dubicka Brda?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I stayed a while, maybe a month.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And from Dubicka Brda, where were you taken then?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: From there we were taken to Hrvatska Dubica where they had their command post and their headquarters. There was Kovacevic, Momcilo and Stela Radjunovic -- rather, Stevo. Correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Going back to Dubicka Brda, which place did you stay? We already heard that it was headquarter, but I am -- I am more interested to know which part of the building you were -- you were kept in.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: They kept us in a private house, in fact in one room of that house where the tank crews and mortar crews and cannon crews slept. And they dedicated one room for prisoners so that they could keep an eye on us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Apart from you two, was there anybody else? Were there some other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, later. Another two or three were brought later.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How were you treated in this headquarter in -- in Dubicka Brda?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: During the day they would take us outside to work, and the work consisted of looting, looting for the Serbs. We looted Croat houses. We would gather all the livestock. And later we worked on the bridge that had been destroyed. During the night they gave us hot meals, as they called it. And it was kept warm, that meal, so that we could continue working tomorrow. And they also kept our bodies warm. That's what they called beatings. And in addition to the beatings, they made us sing songs with lyrics that went something like "Get ready, get ready, Chetniks. There will be a big battle." And we had to run around like in training and sing those songs. They surrounded us in two circles, and we had to run. Everybody had some sort of weapon. Each one of them had a gun, or an axe, and they would use those things to beat us as we run by. When we were completely exhausted and unable to run anymore and our lips were unable to form those words, they would push us to one side and make us run again. And when we were completely exhausted and couldn't move, they would take their guns and pistols and fire to give us inspiration to run some more. There was one of them, Zeljko Abaza -- rather, one of us was called Zeljko Abaza, and one of the bullets grazed him on the hip. I was behind him and helped him up. I asked him, "Can you manage? Is it too bad?" And he said, "I'll go on." There were also interrogations accompanied by music, the Serb song "March on the Drina." I didn't know the meaning of that song, of that music at that time. I remembered it from some sort of movie. He asked me to explain what kind of music it was, and I couldn't answer, so he hit me on the head with a crowbar. There was another -- another one of us whose turn it came to answer the question. He was -- he was also hit on the head. And Abaza was the third one, and he gave the correct answer. He said, "March on the Drina" is the name of the song, but they hit him anyway. And when he got up, they asked him, "How do you know this is it?" And Abaza said, "I just know." There was also Ante Knezevic among us, a man of about 50. He -- he lived through the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you at this moment, but let's take it step-by-step. I will ask you to clarify certain things. You were talking now about the beating, but at the beginning you started talking about looting, that you were looting for Serbs. Who was involved in this looting? And I'm talking who from the Serbs? Which forces were involved in this looting?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: All the Serb forces that I have enumerated so far, be it the JNA or the TO or the police, or the police of SAO Krajina. Everybody took part in the looting. And they made us loot for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Then you started talking about how you were beaten, how you were forced to run until you were exhausted. Was this something which happened in this Serb headquarter in Dubicka Brda, or was it something which happened already in Dubica?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: That happened later in Hrvatska Dubica, in the old school building. Before, that building used to be a school. After that, it was adapted into some sort of farm building or outbuilding. Anyway, they chose it for their command post. When I say "they," I mean Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When kind of command post? Was there a post of TO or police? Who was there? Who did you see there?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whose command post I saw. All kinds of uniforms there. The police, Chetniks, TO. I can't tell you to whom they belonged and what uniforms they wore, whether they were TO or Chetnik or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you see Veljko Radjunovic and Momcilo Kovacevic at this building, at this old school building?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I used to see them there. They were the gang leaders there. They were the ones who issued orders, who decided what would be done.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You then describe how you were beaten. Did these men participate in beating as well?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You started talking about interrogation. What did they question you about?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: They interrogated us about the Croatian army, the Croat police, what kind of weapons they had, how many, where their weapons come from, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And while you were interrogate -- while you were interrogated, were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, every time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And where did -- where did they take you in this building, old school building? Where did you stay?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: They held us in a toilet that was perhaps two metres long and 70 centimetres wide. It was the kind of toilet that didn't have a proper watercloset but a hole in the ground where you had to crouch. There were four of us there, myself, Coric, Knezevic, and Abaza. And I almost forgot to mention the fifth man, Idriz Causevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: While you were kept -- kept in this toilet room, did you have something to sleep on?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. It was a concrete floor. Later they gave us some jackets left behind by the Croatian police. We knew that because they had patches on the sleeves saying "Croatian police."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you get water?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. After a while we got a jerrycan that earlier had oil in it, petrol.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So what kind of water it was? Was it fresh water you get?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was drinkable for us, because we couldn't get hold of any other water. Of course it wasn't clean water. It had remnants of oil in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What did you eat? What kind of food did you receive?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: We got small -- small liver pate packages and two pieces of bread.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's a suitable time for the break --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will take a short break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Before the break we talk about the conditions in the detention place. Now I would like to return to your treatment. I interrupted you when you were talking about how were you made to run, how you were hit over your head. When you were beaten, did you stay conscious all the time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: All the time. In fact, after a while when we were no longer able to withstand that, we would faint.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know whether anybody died in this old school place where you were detained?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Right. When I came to -- before all that, they splashed us with water. It was very cold. And I don't know how much time passed while I was unconscious. And when I came round, I heard the moaning of Mico Coric. He repeated like a mantra, "They will kill us. They will kill us." And that's the first sound that I heard as I was coming to. And I asked him what had happened in the meantime, and he told me. And after that -- in fact, while we were still unconscious, they dragged us back to the toilet where we were held. And when we came to, they took us to a tractor with a trailer, and we had to load two corpses onto the trailer so they can drive to the river and throw them in the water.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: But we were unable to stand on our feet, and we had great difficulty loading the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you recognise who were these would bodies? Who were these people?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. One was Antun Knezevic, and the other was Zeljko Abaza.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: These were the two men who were detained together with you in the toilet?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were you able to see what happened to them, whether they had any injuries?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Since we were unable to stand on our feet, it was them who loaded the bodies onto the trailer, and they told us to get on. We were unable to do that, so they threw us onto the trailer. They ordered us to lie down on top of the bodies. So I ended up lying on the body of Zeljko Abaza. And I could still feel the vibrations through the body.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What -- what else --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the last part. Can he repeat just the few last words?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Josipovic, the interpreters didn't hear the last sentence you said. We understood that you felt the vibrations through the body, but what did you say after that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I said that I had also remarked that he had his throat slit with a knife or something.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You were constantly referring to "they." "They loaded the bodies. They told us." Who were present when you were ordered to load these body on this truck? Who were they?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I mean the Serbs, because there was Stevo Radjunovic, Momcilo Kovacevic, Mirko Sarac, Milan Petrovic, Djordje Ratkovic, Djuro Jerinic, Marjan Prvalo, all Serbs. Mladen Pozar.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And all these were present when you were -- you were ordered to load these bodies on the truck and then when you climb on the truck and lie on -- lied on these bodies?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were all there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Ms. Richterova, before you carry on, may I ask for some clarification, please? The witness has mentioned that a throat was slit. Whose throat was it? Was it Antun or Zeljko's? And earlier on you had asked him about whether there were injuries. He said yes. Could we hear what type of injuries there were? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Josipovic, you heard the Judge. Can you tell us what kinds of injury did you see on these bodies?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw the injuries while I was lying on Zeljko's body. I could see that he had stab wounds and his throat was cut. After we arrived from that yard to the bridge across the Una River where they ordered us again to take the bodies out of the trailer and throw them off the bridge into the water, I noticed that Knezevic Antun also had his throat cut.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What happened to these body -- bodies?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I was ordered to throw them off the bridge, but we were so exhausted that we were not able to lift the bodies. So these Serbs, including Mirko Sarac and Milan Petrovic and all the others, they took the bodies and threw them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just for clarity's sake, is Abaza's first name Zeljko or Veljko? I thought earlier the witness had corrected it to say Veljko, V instead of Z at the beginning. Can we just get that clarified?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was it Zeljko Abaza or Veljko Abaza. Can you please clarify this point?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: It was Zeljko Abaza.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: After these Serb bodies were thrown into river, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: They ordered me to put one leg over the fence and in fact to go on the other side of the fence on the bridge so that they could shoot us and we would end up in the river.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What happened then? Did -- did you end up in the river?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: No. Because at that time a patrol showed up, their own Serb patrol, and stopped them from committing this crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: After they stopped, what happened to you? Where -- where were you taken after that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: We were sent back to the command, to that building and to the toilet, and that's where we stayed until the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And it was you and who else returned?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I and Mico Coric.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You also mentioned before that there was one Idriz Causevic detained together with you in that toilet. Do you know what happened to Idriz Causevic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. About three days earlier, he was taken out of the toilet. We heard moaning, groaning coming from Idriz, and then after a while when it was our turn, when Ante and Zeljko were killed that night, they told us that he had been moaning and groaning. We wondered what would happen to us. He was moaning and wondering what would happen to him. And then we found out that he had been killed. We knew he would never return again.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And did you ever see Idriz Causevic again?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You testified that you and your -- your nephew returned back from that bridge back to the old school building, back to the toilet. What happened after that? How long did you stay in this building?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: After we had returned to the building, they gave us some water and some brooms to wash away the blood with from the asphalt parts. We had to clean up the blood from the asphalt parts. We did that. And once we had done that, we were sent back to the toilet, and we stayed there until the morning. Son was on duty. He spent the entire night there on duty. He observed what was happening throughout the night. Although he did not authorise them to act in the way that they did, he was quite simply helpless. He couldn't do anything for us or for the other two or three individuals whom they killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: After these three men were killed, did they continue with the same treatment as before, I mean the beatings every day, or did something change?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. All sorts of things happened. They took us away to work. We would gather the livestock and drive them to a farm. That's where we drove the livestock to. And at one point in time while we were working we noticed a helicopter. And the Serbs who worked with us, who guarded us and who ordered us to work commented on the event and said that Martic had arrived by helicopter from Krajina. They said that he couldn't come to Hrvatska Dubica, that he had flown over Serbia, that he was keeping to the Serbian side, and they said he would land there and would be driven to Zivaja from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know why he couldn't come to Hrvatska Dubica? Do you know why? Did they explain why he couldn't come to Hrvatska Dubica?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was some sort of a conflict, some sort of a quarrel between the president of the SDS, Mile Misljenovic, and the Jovo Misljenovic. I don't know why there was a quarrel. Apparently their own rebellious Serbs had opened fire on Misljenovic's house and they wanted to kill him. But he managed to flee to Knin. He got away. And he told Martic about what had happened in Hrvatska Dubica. And that's how I know that Martic was present. After a while, they took us to Zivaja, the village of Zivaja, which was inhabited by Serbs, and there was a command there. I found out that Martic was a guest. And they took us to show two Ustashas to him. They took us there so that Martic could see us. After a while they returned. They said Martic didn't want to bother with us. They were going to take us back to Hrvatska Dubica. He didn't want to spoil the fun and the celebration apparently. I don't know what kind of a celebration was on. And they returned us or took us back to Hrvatska Dubica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So you never -- you didn't see Martic in Dubica or Zivaja personally, only heard that he was present?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see him there. I only heard that he was present. That's what the Serbs said. And they told us why they were taking us from Hrvatska Dubica to Zivaja.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: For how long were you detained?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: For five months.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was there any time when the people who detained you and you -- you also stated their name, including Stevo Radjunovic and Kovacevic. Was there a time when these people left or were replaced?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a transfer of power. I don't know on how many occasions. Changes of authority. Some people were thrown out of the command. The JNA, the military police arrived. They took over, and after a certain period of time the JNA and military police were expelled, and they returned to power again and stayed in power.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When you said that some people were thrown out, do you know exactly who was thrown out?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm referring to Momcilo Kovacevic and Stevo Radjunovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You stated that you were detained for about five months. After you were released, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I stayed on in Hrvatska Dubica until the end of November or the beginning of December. And then an officer from the JNA arrived and from the military police. They were going to take me to Prijedor, to a prison in Prijedor. But, in fact, with the help of a Serbian friend of mine, he helped me to save myself. They took me to Prijedor, and I spent some time in Prijedor. I was then transferred to Banja Luka. And after a while, on the 10th of February, 1992, I was exchanged and I went to Slavonski Brod.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to return a little bit back when you were still in prison. First, you mentioned this Kovacevic and Radjunovic, that they were thrown out. Do you know by whom?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. There are all sorts of stories circulated when the JNA arrived, the military police arrived and took power. Well, I don't know who threw them out, who expelled them. It was said that the White Eagles, that Seselj's men had arrived from Belgrade and that they had put the military police and the JNA in power. Naturally, after they left, when they returned to Belgrade these people returned from Bosnia and toppled over the power structure. They expelled the JNA and the military police, and they once again took -- took power, and they were the lords and masters in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: While you were in police, did you learn what happened to people who lived in Croatian villages?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: While you were still in prison [Realtime transcript read in error "police"], did you have opportunity to learn from either soldiers or somebody else what happened to civilian who stayed behind in Croatian villages like Cerovljani, Bacin, Dubica, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I found out that they had been taken away -- rather, they had been assembled in a hall, a club, where they were guarded. And naturally, while we were involved in rounding up the livestock, while we were involved in performing our duties we saw these people. Naturally, we heard from Serbian soldiers who were with us and who were guarding us that they had rounded up these people. Apparently they were going to be exchanged in Glina, but in fact captain first class went to see Mico Coric. He addressed him and told him what had happened on that occasion. And Mico Coric's mother had been placed in that club, in that hall, and taken to Glina for an exchange. But in fact they did not end up in Glina. They were not exchanged. They were taken to Rezani [phoen] near a place called Bacir, and they were killed there. When this captain spoke to Mico Coric, he didn't in fact tell him that is what had happened, but in the course of their conversation he tried to address this matter in an indirect way and tell him what had happened. He tried to insinuate certain things.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: First, I would like to -- there needs to be a correction on page 31, line 24. I asked were you were in prison, and this line says while you were in police. So that needs to be corrected. I think the interpreters also didn't get the name of the place where these people were supposedly killed. You said Bacina -- Bacin. It was near of which place?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: You mean Bazan Knezevic [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No, I apologise. You stated that --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: We're referring to civilians. The place was called Bacin Krecane near Bacin. I've mentioned this place. Krecane near a place called Bacin.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. We just didn't understand, so I wanted you to repeat this -- this place so we have it correctly in the transcript. Do you know approximately how many people were -- were, altogether, killed?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: It's difficult to say. I don't know how many people were killed, but since an exhumation was carried out and it's a mass grave, all those from the Croatian villages and all the people -- well, some of them were identified, whereas others are still recorded as missing. I don't know what the number is, but perhaps about 90 individuals are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And you also mentioned that Mico Coric was asking about his mother, what happened to his mother. Do you know what happened to Mico's -- Mico Coric's mother?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. After Operation Storm and after Croatian authority had been established within the borders of Croatia, an exhumation was performed, and Mico Coric's mother was discovered. Her body was exhumed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you also return to your village after the Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What did you find? How did the village look like?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: When I returned to my village I couldn't recognise it. A lot of things had been destroyed and burnt down. Excavators had been used to remove the rubble of houses. Later I found out that they had transported this through the forest in lorries, and they had made sort of roads there so that they could attack the Croatian defence forces with cannons and tanks and other equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You said that everything was burned down. Were -- were all houses burned down? Were all Serb and Croatian houses, or were there only houses of one of these ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Only Croatian and Muslim houses had been burnt down and destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I concluded my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Richterova. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I am counsel for Milan Martic. I will now be conducting the cross-examination. I assume that you know what this means. To make sure that the interpreters can do their work, I'd be grateful if you could pause once I have put a question to you before answering the question. In the statement you gave to the Prosecution, you said that you were born in Hrvatska Dubica and that you spent your entire life there. You also said that the Croats were in the majority there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... from the statement of the witness, Mr. Milovancevic, and the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We will distribute copies of the statement for all those who are present in the courtroom. Your Honour, the first statement given to the Prosecution is not in English. We have provided you with a copy of this statement. So perhaps I could ask my learned friend for the Prosecution to be of assistance to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We have an English version. Are you referring to 2000 -- 2000?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct. Thank you. May I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may continue if you will please indicate which statement you are using. Is it the 2000 one or the 2002 one?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since there are a number of statements, whenever I put a question to the witness I will specify which statement my question concerns, whether it's the one given in the year 2000 or the one given in the year 2001. I will now put some questions to the witness which won't relate to any particular statements or in which I won't be quoting anything from his statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your testimony, you mentioned the house of your parents in the village of Predore. Where is that village in relation to Hrvatska Dubica? How far away is it from Hrvatska Dubica?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: In my statement and when giving evidence I have already said that my village is eight kilometres from Hrvatska Dubica. I will repeat this if you can't remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you did your military service, your regular military service. When did you do your military service, and was it in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was in 1989 and 1990 in the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you were serving in the military, were there soldiers and officers in the JNA who were members of all the ethnic groups in Yugoslavia, Serbs, Croats, Macedonians, Albanians, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at the time I wouldn't put it in that way. At the time the system was falling apart. It was breaking up. The Serbs and the Serbian army were in power, although it was called the Yugoslav army. But at the time I was in Kosovo, and problems had arisen with the Albanians in Kosovo, and it was possible to notice, although I wasn't a soldier at the time, the JNA were using force. I had to serve in their army. And at the time, Slovenia wasn't allowing its inhabitants to cross the Slovenian border and to do their military service outside of Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, already in 1989 when you were doing your military service, problems with Albanians in Kosovo were already in evidence. What kind of problems?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you what kind, but I can tell you that already in 1990, in end December and all the way up to March 1990, while I was doing my military service, we all knew what was going to happen, what the JNA was, and what it was all about. I sensed this very clearly. And many officers often told me, in very obscene terms, that I am Tudjman's motherfucker. Stipe Mesic was then the Croat president. They didn't let him assume his post in the Presidency. And all of us who were non-Serbs realised what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said in 1989 and 1990 the Slovene leadership wasn't allowing its conscripts to do the military service.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: They didn't want them to serve outside the borders of Slovenia. I don't know why exactly this came about, but from my understanding they could no longer agree who was going to be president of the former Yugoslavia, whether a Slovene or a Croat or a Bosnian or an Albanian or a Serb would be the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We now move to a subject that I wasn't intending to raise, and I don't really want to extend your testimony to what is not covered by your statement. Tell me just one thing: In 1990, is it the case that Stipe Mesic was a member of the Presidency, being a Croat? The Prime Minister was also a Croat, Ante Markovic? The chief commander of the air force was a Slovene? His name was Anton Tus. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not a politician. I don't want to talk about things I don't know and who occupied which post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Regarding the army, because you happened to be doing your military service right at that time in 1990, I'll ask you one more question. Apart from the JNA, which was the regular army, you mentioned that there was also the Territorial Defence in existence.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. In the times of Yugoslavia, it existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Would I be right in saying that according to the laws and the constitution of Yugoslavia each republic, each autonomous province and even each local commune had its own Territorial Defence and that all ethnicities were included in this Territorial Defence, all who were able to carry a rifle?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if you would be right, but that was how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your testimony covers the period from 1990 onwards. You said that up to 1990, in fact until the elections, human relations, regardless of ethnicity, were good.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you could say that. All the way up to the elections. But once the elections were over and when Croatia formed its own government, those people who served in the police, depending on which ethnicity they belonged to, wore different emblems. Croats wore the chequer-board emblem and Serbs continued with the five-pointed star.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mean to say that after the 1990 elections the Croatian authorities insisted on their own independent state, whereas Serbs insisted on continuing to wear the five-pointed star that symbolised the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Elections were held in Dubica in 1990 like in other places. Can you tell us if it is the case that the greatest majority of the people in Dubica voted HDZ?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who they voted for, but I know the HDZ won the elections, the Croat Democratic Union.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement given to the OTP in 2000, page 2, paragraph 6, you mention that soon after the elections in 1990 Croats stepped out of the Territorial Defence and formed their own Home Guards Corps, ZNG, as a separate armed formation.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I no longer remember what I stated five or six years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: But is it true? Did it happen this way? The Croats left the Territorial Defence after the elections in 1990 and established the ZNG, the Home Guards Corps?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: If I said that and if it's recorded in the statement, there is no reason to retract from that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that Croat residents stepped out of the Territorial Defence that covered the entire population of Yugoslavia, does it mean that they left it of their own will?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that Croats stepped out of the Territorial Defence after the elections in 1990, and I'm asking you does this mean that they left of their own free will?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what would be more correct to say, that they were expelled or that they left on their own free will. It's true that they left and that after that they formed their own police force and their ZNG, the Home Guards Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, can I ask that you give each other space between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'll pay more attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You have stated to the OTP in your first statement that after the 1990 elections the Home Guards Corps was established, and its commander for the region was Tomislav Mateljak. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On page 2, paragraph 8 of your first statement to the OTP from the year 2000 you mentioned that you personally thought of Mateljak as a criminal, unemployed scum who had lived in a shanty in Dubica before the war, and he came into power during the war. He became powerful.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Also in paragraph 8, you say that Mateljak was in charge of organising and arming the Croats. Do you mean to say the Croat population there?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement to the OTP from year 2000 in the seventh paragraph you say that after the ZNG was established, the relationship between Serbs and Croats in the village started to change, that the first signs of mistrust between the two sides appeared, and they started to fear each other. Nobody felt safe anymore.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I said that. After the Croats formed their authorities, however, the Serbs continued on the police force, but they did not accept the new emblem of the Croatian state, the chequer-board. They continued to wear the five-pointed star, and the Croatian authorities would not allow this kind of inconsistence. They tried to enforce their new emblem, and Serbs of course didn't give in. They went to the woods, became renegades, and started to form their own units, some Chetnik units on the pretext that they represented the defence forces of the old Yugoslavia, namely the TO, the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, we'll come to the JNA and the TO later. Let us now stick to these developments in your village. You stated earlier today, and it's in your statement, too, that Serbs would go across the Una River to spend the night in Bosanska Dubica, and they would return every morning. But now you also say that they spread false rumours and they returned during the day.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I said. They went to Bosnia, across the river. They spread propaganda. They lied to the JNA and the military police in order to make the JNA believe, and other Serbs as well, that it's necessary to topple the new Croatian authorities and to enable them to be back with their five-pointed stars and cockades. When I say that they went across the river to Bosnia, I mean to say that they were going there to solicit assistance, to present themselves as being in jeopardy. And their actions actually put them in danger and the whole of Croatia in danger, because it was causing a quarrel between Croatia and the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is that your position, your understanding of what happened?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: No. It's just what happened. It's the reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you talk about those Serbs who went during the night to Bosnia, who were they? Grown men, women, elderly men? Who went to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What kind of people went to Bosanska Dubica during the night to return in the morning? Who were they? Men, women?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: No. Women and children stayed at home because they didn't think they were in danger. They didn't think it necessary to go and spend the night in Bosnia. Able-bodied younger men went across, people who were able to carry a gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Some witnesses we've heard earlier mentioned women and children going to Bosnia, but you are saying something entirely different. So I'm going to ask you what you meant when saying that Serbs spread false rumours. Do you mean to say that the arming of the Croat population in Hrvatska Dubica after the elections in 1990 was in the hands of a man whom you yourself called the criminal, and how can it be perceived in a mixed community?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Whatever I thought of him, I didn't think of him as a war criminal and a murderer. That was simply my opinion of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement to the OTP, again paragraph 8, you said the situation changed dramatically after the Territorial Defence arrested some Croats, including this Tomislav Mateljak, and Predrag Vucicevic. What was Vucicevic's ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said about Vucicevic that he had joined the police after the Serbs left the police force. Does that mean that he was admitted to replace some Serb policemen who left?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. But in fact, not necessarily, because he had been a policeman before. He had served on the police force while Serb policemen were still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that those people who were arrested were taken by a civilian truck to Kostajnica, that Mateljak managed to escape on the way, whereas Vucicevic was exchanged for a Serb who had been captured. Who captured that Serb?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: The Croat police or the Croat army. I don't know who. What mattered was that one Serb was captured and that was enough for the exchange with Vucicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement to the OTP from year 2000, paragraph 10, you said that Serbs operating in the region wore the olive-drab uniforms of the JNA or green camouflage uniforms with the insignia of SAO Krajina, a crown and a cross with four S's in Cyrillic letters. Did you state that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. May I ask the Honourable Trial Chamber for a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In view of this request and looking at the clock as well, could we -- or maybe I am premature in asking for a break. Yes. I see now that it's my mistake, that we are to go on a break on only 15 past 5.00, but maybe we can take into account what the witness just asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The witness asks for a break, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness asked for the break, and I thought it coincided with our regular break anyway, but I was wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just want to inform that this witness flew in today after -- after working yesterday, so I assume that he must be very tired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Can we take a break for -- our normal break for 30 minutes, and then we will come back at half past 5.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic. Just before you proceed, Mr. Milovancevic. Is the witness in a position to carry on until the end of the day, 7.00 today?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, you will have to ask. I have no contact. I'm not allowed to have contact with the witness. We only informed VWU that he wasn't feeling well, or, let us say, he was tired, but I haven't received any further information on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Witness, can I just ask, are you -- do you feel in a position to go on? We're supposed to knock off at 7.00 tonight. Can you make that? And if you can't, please say so that we break off at some stage to give you time to take a break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can continue. It's not a problem. Everything is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. But just do mention it when you need a break. Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'll now continue with my cross-examination. If you feel you need a break, please don't hesitate to inform us of the fact.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I'll do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When describing the circumstances under which you joined the ZNG, you said it was in the summer of 1991. Is that correct, Witness?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the statement that you gave to the Prosecution in the year 2000 on page 3, paragraph 12, you stated that towards the end of July, 1991, you and your brother Dragan and your cousin Mico Coric went to Kutina because you were not members of the HDZ and you didn't want to fight anyone. However, the Croatian police found you and returned you to Dubica and said that you had to join the ZNG. Is that in fact what happened?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
