utterances.text: I don't know which month that happened in. It's difficult for me to remember exactly what I said, but that is in fact what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the summer of 1991 when you returned from Kutina to Dubica, who else was active apart from the ZNG? Which other Croatian forces were in existence? Were there any members of the Croatian police?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: When I returned from Kutina, there were Serb members of the police force. They were still members of the police force at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were these policemen part of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: They should have been part of that ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At the time was there a local police station in Hrvatska Dubica, in the summer of 1991, and before that time? I'm referring to the period 1990 to 1991.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. From the period of the former Yugoslavia. It was the former police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You're referring to the Yugoslav police; is that correct? Does that mean that the Croatian Ministry of the Interior in 1991 took over the police station that had previously existed, that had existed in the -- the former Yugoslavia, in Hrvatska Dubica? Is that what you are claiming?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Apart from the ZNG and the so-called local police force, the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior in Dubica, were there any other Croatian policemen who came from outside, from other areas in Dubica?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were very few of them, very few policemen who had actually trained as policemen, but there were some.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the statement that you gave to the Prosecution in the year 2000, on page 3, paragraph 14, you said that Croatian policemen from Moslavina were at the bridge and that they ordered you to open sniper fire on soldiers who were on the other side of the river. Is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were policemen from Moslavina there, and I don't know from which other parts of Croatia they came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At the time you were a member of the ZNG. Were you issued with a uniform and a weapon?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I had some sort of a rusty weapon, but I didn't have a uniform at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the statement you gave to the Prosecution in the year 2000 paragraph 13 on page 3, you said that you thought that all HZD [as interpreted] members had uniforms. You said that you didn't have a uniform but that all members of the HZD had uniforms at the time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, one could say so. Some had such uniforms, but there were others who didn't. Not everyone had a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where these uniforms and weapons came from, the uniforms and weapons that were distributed?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's a very difficult question. I really wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you became a member of the ZNG, you said that Tomislav Mateljak issued a sniper rifle to you. It had a sight, a scope, a sniper scope. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the continuation of the statement that you gave to the Prosecution in the year 2000, you explained that you refused to obey the orders issued to you by the Croatian police men from Moslavina. They ordered you to open fire on the soldiers on the other side of the river and after your refusal Mateljak took your rifle from you and you were reassigned to work in the kitchen. Is that correct? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This statement that we have been referring to, the statement that you gave to the Prosecution in the year 2000, you also said that several days after this event with the sniper rifle you were informed of the fact that Stojan Bekic's house was on fire. What was the ethnicity of Bekic and where was his house located?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Stojan Bekic, he was a Serb. He had a house in Hrvatska Dubica. And in my village, the village of Predore, he had a ranch, and his ranch was on fire and a little house on the ranch.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know why his house had been set on fire? Do you know what the cause of the fire was?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know why it was on fire. I don't know how -- how the house caught fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the statement that you gave to the Prosecution in the year 2000, you said that when you heard that Bekic's house was on fire you went to the village of Predore and the local inhabitants had said that they had seen a JNA helicopter land near the house. They had delivered a lot of weapons that were taken the neighbouring Serbian villages of Zivaja and Sas. They were taken there by lorry. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, what I said about Stojan Bekic, yes, I didn't know that his house was on fire, but I was informed that there was a house on fire in the village of Predore. I didn't know that it was his house. But when we arrived in the village, we heard that the house in question was in fact Stojan Bekic's house or, rather, it was his ranch that was concerned. That's what we heard and that's what we saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So what you have just said explains why you went to the village of Predore. You heard that there was a fire there and you went to see your mother's house. Have I understood you correctly? And then you realised what had happened there once you reached the village. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. You're quite right about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You haven't answered my question about how the inhabitants told you that they had seen that a helicopter had landed in the vicinity of their houses, a helicopter with a lot of weapons. When you were in Predore, when this house was on fire, did the inhabitants tell you that they had seen this helicopter with the weapons?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: No. That's not what I said. I didn't say that the inhabitants had told me that they had seen this helicopter, that my mother and a neighbour had told me that a helicopter had landed in the forest. I said that I had seen the helicopter and the weapons. I didn't say that it was the inhabitants who had seen the helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Witness. That was your evidence today. However, in the statement that you gave to the Prosecution in the year 2000, you in fact said that when you went to the village of Predore because of the fire that was there, the inhabitants told you that a JNA helicopter had landed and that weapons had been unloaded from the helicopter. Is that what you stated to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps that is what I stated to the Prosecution, but perhaps an error was made. The fire took place in the evening hours. And after I had arrived there, the inhabitants told me and my mother told me that a helicopter had flown over during the day. A helicopter had flown over the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, this is not your problem, but we do have a slight problem. You keep referring to the number of the paragraph. The English version is not numbered, and we find it very difficult to follow. I'm particularly interested to see in his statement on this point that you are now talking about. Could you tell us how the paragraph begins?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would just like to tell you that we received the statement from the Prosecution, and each paragraph is marked in pencil in order to make it easier to find our bearings. I'll tell you where this paragraph is. When I say paragraph, well, in fact, these are just various passages so that we can find on various pages. The part of the text that I was referring to when questioning the witness is on page 3 of the B/C/S version of the statement, the statement given to the Prosecution in November 2000. It's the last paragraph at the bottom of the page. The number is 02964236. So the passage starts with the words: "After that I was transferred to the kitchen," and then the text that follows describes the fire in Predore and the visit to his mother. That is the paragraph I was referring to. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I was just trying to refer to what you stated in your statement, and I think it doesn't quite tally with your evidence given today. This is why I'm asking you what is in fact correct. You said that you went to visit your mother when this fire occur. You said that you reached your family house. Your mother was afraid, and the inhabitants said that they had seen a JNA helicopter landing in the vicinity of the houses. JNA was inscribed on the helicopter, and many weapons were loaded onto a civilian lorry from the helicopter, civilian lorry that belonged to Electra. The civilian inhabitants saw this lorry transferring the weapons to the neighbouring Serbian villages of Zivaja and Sas. And now my question is: Do you remember having given such a statement to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that statement very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ms. Richterova was on her feet. Can we hear what she's got to say, Mr. Milovancevic. Yes, Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In fact, I referred to Mr. Milovancevic's question, what is correct that what he said today is something different what is in his statement from 2000 and -- from 2000, and I just want to refer to his statement from 2002 in which he says that he saw it. And to that effect, he testified today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Richterova. Maybe that's something you could have raised in re-examination. It's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell me whether these neighbours of yours told you how it was that they knew that this Electra lorry was transporting the weapons to the villages of Sas and Zivaja? Did they tell you how they knew that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that they told me that they had seen the weapons. I'll repeat this. I don't remember having said that the local people told me that they had seen the helicopter delivering weapons. I said that I had seen that, but the local people said that prior to that event on a number of occasions a helicopter had landed at the same site. And as I have already said, on one occasion when I was going home my mother told me that a helicopter had landed than it was there. I went and saw what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me how far the village of Zivaja is from Predore and in which direction is the village located?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not quite sure what you mean when you say in which direction it is. You mean to the south, to the east, to the north? I think it's to the north from my village, from the village of Predore. And if you take the path that goes through the forest, it's perhaps 15 or 20 kilometres away. Perhaps less than that. And if you go through my village, then it would be about six or seven kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your second statement to the OTP from 2002, on page 2, in what I would call paragraph 2, you said that JNA helicopters carrying ammunition and weapons landed in the forest near Zivaja and Sas villages, several occasions, and then their load would be transferred by trucks to surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't say Zivaja and Sas. I said they landed near my village only 600 metres away from the village itself and then they probably transferred the load by trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean by "probably"?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: That means that I was there and saw with my own eyes what that helicopter was doing and what was going on, and I concluded that on all the other occasions they came, they came for the same purpose, to bring weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say that you concluded that as soon as the helicopter came there their mission was to bring weapons. Did you look as it happened?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I'll tell you this again: My mother told me that the helicopter had come several times before. So I went to the woods to see for myself what was going on when the helicopter lands. And indeed, they transferred the load, the weapons and ammunition to Electra company trucks, and all the other things that I've already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that those villages, Zivaja and Sas, to which the weaponry was destined was several kilometres away from the landing site. Can you explain to me why the helicopter didn't land right in that village, Zivaja or Sas? Why would the trucks go 10 kilometres back and forth?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't answer that. I couldn't quite understand myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You also said that those trucks and pickups drove the weapons to Zivaja and Sas. Did you ever go to Zivaja and Sas to see those trucks arrive carrying weapons?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not. But I know very well that those same weapons were brought to Hrvatska Dubica as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At that time when you became member of the ZNG, when you were on the bridge and when you were issued with a sniper, you were a member of the ZNG, and you spent very little time in your own village.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So how can you say that in the period when the helicopter landed in Zivaja and Sas it occurred almost on a daily basis if you yourself were in Dubica?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I told you that I went several times to visit my mother and that my mother told me about it. And I'm telling you again the helicopter didn't land in Zivaja or Sas. It landed about 800 metres from my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does all this mean, Witness, that it is on the basis of your mother's words and what you heard from other people that you concluded the helicopters were carrying weapons?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: What was I supposed to conclude, that they were carrying crisps?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement to the OTP, page 2000 [as interpreted], paragraph 17 as I marked it. That would be the third paragraph from top of the page. You said that on the order of Croatian President Franjo Tudjman Tomislav Mateljak ordered the Croat population to be evacuated from Dubica and surrounding villages. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That happened sometime after Dvor Na Uni and Hrvatska Kostajnica fell. Maybe two or three days later the order came that we, the Croatian army, the ZNG, were too weak to keep Hrvatska Dubica under control and that we had to withdraw before the Chetniks, the JNA and all the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is -- was that an order to the effect that civilians should withdraw or that you, the troops, should withdraw?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what the order exactly was, but first of all civilians were to retreat and then the troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where the civilians went from Hrvatska Dubica?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I know they went to Jasenovac, across the Sava River towards Moslavina. They found places to stay just to be able to survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: After the civilians left Dubica, did the Croatian police and members of the ZNG remain?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I said after the civilians left Hrvatska Dubica, did Croat policemen and members of the Home Guards Corps remain in Dubica?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: No, they did not. They, too, pulled out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned in your statement that Serb positions were then shelled by the Croat side from a moving train.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I said there were mortars mounted on the train, and I explained what their purpose was. They had no precision to speak of, and they could hardly even reach the Serb positions with their range. It was more of a propaganda move and perhaps designed to gain some time to pull out the Croatian population, and the Serbs were victims of their own propaganda, and they were fanning their own fears.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You just said that mortar shells fired from the moving train were a propaganda move.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: No. I said that that was meant to secure a retreat, to sort of gain time before the Serbs, to intimidate them a little so that Croat civilians and troops have time to move out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that it was Tudjman's order to pull out the civilian population, that Mateljak passed this order on, and that the train continued firing even after that was done.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Ask me something easier. I've told you this many times, that an order came from Tudjman that we did have enough men, we didn't have the kind of weapons that would repel the Serb aggression, and that we had to retreat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said in your statement and in your testimony earlier today that at one point the bridge near Hrvatska Dubica was destroyed. When and who destroyed it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Croatian troops and Croatian police, because as they were running away before JNA tanks and howitzers, they destroyed the bridge in order to prevent Serb reinforcements and JNA reinforcements to come from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry about this. Did I interrupt you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Would I be right if I remind you that the bridge was destroyed on the night of the 13th September 1991? That's what you testified. Does that date mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course it means something to me. On that night, that date when the bridge was destroyed, there was shooting from the Bosnian side on several occasions. On the Croatian side they fired on churches as well. The Croat side was targeted from mortars. Shells were hitting houses, the road, the church. Cannons were firing at the church. JNA aeroplanes broke the sound barrier, and walls cracked and windows were shattered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that Croats held power and all the official positions in Hrvatska Dubica. You said that Hrvatska Dubica had a headquarters of the ZNG, that it was an Assembly point for Dubica, Bacin, and Cerovljani units of the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the defence sense. We had defence structures in Cerovljani, Dubica and Bacin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, that's September 1991. The Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was still in existence together with its federal army, the JNA. So who was the ZNG defending in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: You mean who was it defending? Is that some sort of provocation, this question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: No, it didn't certainly, but if you don't like it, we'll move on to another one.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you are describing the situation surrounding the destruction of the bridge, would you say that the Croatian police destroyed the bridge between Bosanska Dubica and Hrvatska Dubica to prevent the JNA tanks from crossing?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you didn't ask me who was manning those JNA tanks. Do you want me to answer? Or perhaps you know the answer already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I know that that -- at that time the president of the Yugoslav Presidency was Stjepan Mesic and the federal Prime Minister was another Croat, Ante Markovic. But as for your statement to the OTP from 2000, on page 4 you said that on the 15th of September, 1991, around 50 persons of Serb ethnicity wearing green camouflage uniforms and olive-green uniforms of the JNA surrounded the Predore village. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Which date did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: It's actually you who said that it was on the 15th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said earlier in your testimony, and it's also in both your statements, that you recognised among them Momcilo Kovacevic, Stevo Radjunovic, and Veljko Radjunovic. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and many others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said they searched houses and that those among you who had weapons had discarded those weapons earlier.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were two hunting rifles, and they had been thrown into a well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said they were making inquiries about the presence of soldiers or policemen in the village, about the kind of weapons they had and the presence of heavy weaponry on the Croat side.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I said they were pushing us in front of them like a live shield. They were forcing us to the bank of the Sava River. On the other side of the Sava River, there was Drenov Bog village. They asked us about the population of that village, and I said I didn't know and that they should look for themselves, which they did. And I told them, "You can have a look and decide for yourselves how big the village is, how densely it's populated," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also stated that after you were arrested eight of you were taken to the old school building which housed, as you put it, the Serb command in Hrvatska Dubica.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say eight of us were taken there. I said Mico Coric and I were taken there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Both today and in your statement of year 2000 on page 5, you said at one point you were sent to repair the bridge. Is that the bridge between Hrvatska Dubica and Bosanska Dubica that had been destroyed by the Croatian police in September 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the statement you said that there were some Serbs who were also involved in repairing the bridge together with you. Were they prisoners too?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: The Serbs who worked with me, well, yes, they were Serbs naturally, but they weren't prisoners. They were convicts. They had fled from Lipki, Daruvar, Pacrevac [phoen], from the battlefield, and I don't know from which other places they had fled. They were punished and they been taken to work with us on the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the statements you gave to the OTP in the year 2000, on page 5 you say that Idriz Causevic was taken away one day. You heard moaning. You assume that he was killed, but you didn't see who committed the act. You also said that the following morning you heard the Serbs saying that someone had been killed and that they were quarreling about this. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. I said that one evening before Knezevic was killed and Abaza perhaps two nights earlier on was taken to Causevce [phoen]. We heard groaning, screams, moaning, and he never returned after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That's what my question was about. Did you mention the fact that on the following morning you heard some Serbs who said that someone had been killed and they were quarreling about this? And this has to do with the death of Idriz Causevic.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: No, you're not right. In my statement, I said that there was a quarrel among the Serbs when Ante Knezevic and Zeljko Abaza were killed. They shouldn't have been killed. They were supposed to be exchanged. That's what the quarrel was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And in your statement to the OTP in the year 2000, on page 5 you also said that the people who took you out into the courtyard when this was happening with Ante Knezevic and Zeljko Abaza broke down the door to the room that you were being kept in because they probably couldn't get hold of the key from the duty officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: That happened at night, and that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see who killed Antun Knezevic and Zeljko Abaza?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You described in detail what happened to the bodies of Ante Knezevic and Zeljko Abaza. You said how they were thrown into a river, and on page 6 of your statement to the OTP given in the year 2000 you also said that someone told the people who were around you that they should stop. They even opened fire in your direction. And then the Serbs at the checkpoint put you in the car around returned you to the room you were being kept in. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When they had thrown Abaz and Knezevic into the River Una, we were ordered to go to the other side of the fence, and they were supposed to open fire on us, to kill us so that we, too, would fall into the river. They didn't want to dirty their hands with us. And at that point in time you hear the screech of tires. Some sort of a civilian vehicle arrived, and a quarrel broke out between those who had killed these men and the patrol that had arrived. It was probably some sort of patrol. I don't know who they were. They said that they shouldn't kill the two of us. They said that we would be used in an exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On page 7 of the statement that you gave to the OTP in the year 2000, it's the last paragraph, I think, you say that you think that the killings in the village of Bacin, Hrvatska Dubica, Predore, Tanac, Visnjica and Zivaja were killings that were ordered by Stevo Radjunovic and Momcilo Kovacevic. Do you remember having made such a statement?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember having stated that. Momcilo Kovacevic and Stevo Radjun. They were the big shots there. That's what they thought they were, and that was the case at the time in Hrvatska Dubica. Whatever was done was something that they ordered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Something -- this was something that I wanted to ask you about. The last sentence of yours in the statement to the Prosecution in the year 2002, you said that these two men, Stevo Radjunovic and Momcilo Kovacevic were at the head of all the Serbian forces in that area. In paragraph 3 of that statement, you said that the Territorial Defence formed the Serbian forces. And in paragraph 6, you said that it was difficult for you to distinguish the Territorial Defence from Martic's Police and that you thought that they were a single force and that in fact the same people, the same men would only change their uniforms. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The people were the same. Perhaps they were a little younger. There was the police force, the reconnaissance force, special forces, whereas these other men would change their insignia. It was difficult to distinguish whether someone was a policeman. And I think I have already mentioned this. It was difficult to distinguish whether someone was a policeman, a Territorial Defence member, a member of a reconnaissance unit, a Chetnik, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On page 6 of the statement that you gave to the OTP in the year 2000 you said that at one point in time the JNA and the military police of the JNA took control of the area, not the local Serbs. Do you remember when this happened, roughly speaking? You said that it was about a week after about 90 people had been killed in Krecane. Do you remember having made such a statement?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't agree with that. I don't mean to say that it's just nonsense, but I can't remember whether I in fact made such a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned Krecane and the people who were killed there, do you have in mind the people whose corpses were discovered in Bacin?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: When the exhumation was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When did you find out about the fact these people had been killed? Immediately or was it subsequent to the event?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I think some time had passed after the event. It was when we were carrying out our work, doing what I have already mentioned. There were Bosnians, Serbs who would cross over and who would talk about things. On one occasion when we were working on the bridge, we established contact. The Serbs asked us who we were, the Serbian troops, the Chetniks. I don't know what to call them. So we established contact, we spoke to each other, and at one point they said that you would hear screaming and moaning in the place called Bacin, in the Krecane area. And there was another story. I'm telling you what I heard. I didn't see anything myself. There was another story that was spread. They said that there was a foul stench that was spreading around the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement to the Prosecution in the year 2000, on page 7 you said that you knew that Martic came from Knin on a number of occasions and that he met Radjunovic and Kovacevic. You said that on one occasion while you were rounding up the livestock you heard the guards mention Milan Martic's name, and they mentioned the fact that they had arrived in a helicopter that you saw. You said that you heard the guards saying that that helicopter was to land in the village of Zivaja. Is that what you in fact stated in the year 2000? Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that very well, and you are not correct. I didn't say that Martic met Kovacevic and Radjunovic. I said that he -- this is what the Serbs said amongst themselves and I listened to what they said. I heard that he was visiting the field. He wasn't allowed or he couldn't land in Zivaja but they said that he would land at the railway station in Hrvatska Dubica and that he would be then transported by vehicle to see Misljenovic and Mile.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That was the first statement you gave with regard to Martic and his alleged meetings with Radjunovic and Kovacevic. This was in your statement in the year 2000. In the year 2002, you provided a supplement to your statement. That was on the 17th of November, 2002. And in the second statement, you said that you heard that Martic had gone to Dubica on a number of occasions. And in the middle of October, 1991, you saw a helicopter landing near the railway station in Dubica, and the guards told you that Martic was arriving on that day and that he had left Dubica to go to Zivaja on at that day. However, on that occasion when you saw the helicopter, you did not see Martic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I saw the helicopter, naturally I didn't see Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In this same statement from the year 2002, you said that no one told you what the purpose of his visit was, so you could only assume that he had come to talk to Kovacevic and Radjunovic about the situation in the field. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember. I couldn't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your second supplementary statement from the month of March 2002, on page 3, paragraph 2, you say that Momcilo Kovacevic and Stevo Radjunovic worked in accordance with Milan Martic's orders whose headquarters were based in Knin. "I heard that Kovacevic Stevo Radjunovic would often go to Knin to see Milan Martic and to receive instructions from him. That's what some friends told me." Is that what you in fact stated in this second supplementary statement?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember having made such a statement, but perhaps I said something to that effect. But I don't think that I said he went to get his orders there. And I don't remember saying that Kovacevic and Radjunovic went to see Martic to receive orders but that they would receive orders from Knin, from Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your second supplementary statement from the year 2002, in paragraph 3 on page 3 it says at the end of paragraph 3: "I saw his helicopter arriving in the middle of October 1991." You say that it landed in the vicinity of the railway station in Hrvatska Dubica. And finally you say: "I am sure that this was before the mass execution of civilians in Bacin." Is that what you in fact said?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. If that's what it says in the statement, then that's probably what I said. That's probably what I stated. But I didn't see it landing. I heard that a helicopter would land. I did see a helicopter, and I observed the helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What I've just been quoting was from your supplementary statement given in March 2002, after you had given your first statement to the OTP. Now I want to refer to your third supplementary statement, which was compiled on the 2nd and 3rd of June, 2003. And you say in that statement on page 1 of that supplementary statement that you gave to the Prosecution in 2003, with regard to paragraph 3 you say that you want to add that the 90 people killed in Krecane were civilians. "I heard about this from my cousin Mico Coric." In paragraph 36 you say: "I would like to say that I knew that two local Serbian commanders, Radjunovic and Kovacevic, were fighting for power with the local president of the SDS, Stevo Misljenovic. They even attacked him. I heard that after the attack he went to see Martic in Knin. While I was working in the field during my captivity, on one occasion I saw a helicopter arriving. The local Serbs who were guarding us said that the -- that Martic was arriving to deal with the situation and to relieve those two commanders of their duties, which is what happened very rapidly." Do you remember having given such a statement in your supplementary statement to the OTP in the year 2003?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. This is too detailed for me. There's something I wouldn't agree with in what you have just said. You mentioned Mico Coric, that he apparently told me about Krecane, about Bacin, but I'm not quite clear about your question. Could you put a brief question to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm only asking you about a conflict between Radjunovic and Kovacevic and Misljenovic, and you said that Martic arrived to deal with the situation. That's what the local Serbs said. You said that he had come to relieve these two commanders of their duties. Is that what you said in the statement you gave to the OTP in 2003? Is this contained in the pile of paper that you have before you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. That's what I believed. That's what I thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you that in your first supplementary statement from the year 2002 you said that none of the local guards told you about the purpose of Martic's visit. And now in your supplementary statement, in your third supplementary statement, you say that the guards told you that they had come to deal with the situation and to relieve the two commanders of their duties. What is in fact correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please slow down a bit? Because it's quite obvious that you are trying to confuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I will slow down, but I'm not trying to confuse you. All I am doing is saying that you've described Martic's alleged arrival in a helicopter in one way. In your statement in 2002, you say you don't know what the purpose of his visit was and that the guards hadn't told you about the purpose of his visit, but in your supplementary statement to the Prosecution in 2003 you say that Martic had come to relieve these two individuals of their duties because that's what the guards had told you. So you're describing the same event in two different ways. So what is in fact correct? What you said in 2002, or what you said in 2003, or are both versions correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: It's correct that I cannot remember, and I don't know what I said 15 or 16 years ago, and after 10 or 12 years, and that's the time that has passed since the event -- well, it's difficult for me to remember everything, and I don't even feel the need to remember what I said when I gave the statement in 2002 or when I said -- when I stated something in 1992. You don't have to compare this with what I said in 2002 if what I said in 2002 was somewhat different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, do you have a copy of this statement of 2003 and does the witness have a copy of it? The Bench has two copies. In fact, only I have two copies. The other two Judges have got only one, the statement of 2002. They don't have the statement of 200. But the statement of 2003, it doesn't look like we have. Maybe it might help the witness to jog his memory if he looks at his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'll try to have a constructive approach as far as I can. This supplementary statement given by the witness on the 2nd and 3rd of June, 2003, is marked 02964254 in B/C/S, and it's two pages long. On page 2 we have the signature of the witness. In English, it's marked 02964257. On the first page of this English text ending with numbers 257, that's a subsequent statement of Witness Josipovic, paragraphs 4 and 5, looking from the bottom, paragraphs 36 and 33 are mentioned. I put to the witness his own paragraph 36 describing how two local commanders, Radjunovic and Kovacevic, struggling with Misljenovic, SDS leader, attacked him, after which he went to Knin to see Martic, and Martic, according to the words of the local Serb guards, came and replaced these two commanders. That was his way of dealing with the situation. That is the statement that I'm now putting to the witness as something stated to the Prosecution in 2003. The witness says he doesn't remember it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that. Does the witness have a copy of that statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, did you manage to find your supplementary statement from 2003?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, if you will look at page 1. In the upper right corner the number should end with 254. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, move to the passage mentioning paragraph 36. It refers to this event involving commanders Radjunovic and Kovacevic and their conflict with Misljenovic. You can read it, not aloud, and just tell us if you can confirm giving that statement.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: What exactly is your question concerning paragraph 36?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you state this to the Prosecutor in 2003? Is that what you know?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It also says in this paragraph: "I heard that after this attack he went to see Martic in Knin."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So you read this text regarding paragraph 36, and you are confirming that you described it that way?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: However, you went on to give a fourth supplement to your statement to the OTP on the 12th of March, 2006, and you mentioned it today in the examination-in-chief. This supplement, this addendum, is very brief. It says that in November 1991 there was an incident in which a van carrying Serbs drove over a mine. The driver was seriously wounded and succumbed to his wounds later in Belgrade. And after his death, Martic came to Zivaja village, and he wanted to see Croat prisoners. And you were brought to Zivaja, actually, to be presented to -- to be shown to him, but then he changed his mind. Did you say this -- today?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if that's in the statement. The van did drive over a mine, but who actually laid the mine and who was killed in Serb ranks and who was in the van I can't tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You see, I'm asking you only about this passage related to Martic's alleged visit to Zivaja village in November. Do you stand by your statement that in November 1991, Martic did indeed visit Zivaja as you describe?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe. Maybe in November. But it was several days after this van driver over a mine and after that Serb got killed. That Serb was an important man in Zivaja, held a high position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Witness. I'm just asking you this: Did you hear that Martic visited Zivaja in November?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: That's what people told me. And when this man was killed, that Serb who was in the van, that night they killed Abaza and Knezevic by cutting their throats, and then they drove us to Zivaja. I think it was not actually the same night but one night two or three days later that we were driven to Zivaja when we were told that Martic was in this command post and all the other things that I have already described.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You see, you gave your first statement to the Prosecution in November 2000. Then you were added to it in March 2002. You added to it again in June 2003, describing how Martic came to resolve the conflicts between local leaders Radjunovic, Kovacevic and Misljenovic, and then in 2002 you say -- sorry, in 2003 you say you don't know why he came. And then you made another addendum in 2006. You gave six different statements to the Prosecution. I'm asking you, on the 1st of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter missed the date. We're very sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I have this Official Note of your interview to the police administration of Sisak on the 1st April of 1992 recording your personal details and recording the contents of their interview with you. It contains a lot of information on three pages, including the signature of the person who made this Official Note. This statement is ERN number R0114473, and in English it's R0184936. I want to show you something from that statement. You were exchanged in February 1992, and just a month and a half later, in the same year, you give a statement, and it says: "Momcilo Kovacevic is the commander and Stevo is his deputy. Local Chetniks have control over that area, and they are in conflict with Martic's men. Local Chetniks are responsible for the crimes committed against civilians, looting, torching, et cetera, where as the military police is trying to restore some order and discipline. When in November 1991 Milan Martic came to visit the area, he was in Zivaja, but he didn't dare to go to Dubica. Later on, military police managed to seize control nevertheless. In the meantime, there were several changes of authority." I'm asking you now: Did you give this statement in the police administration in 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if that's what's written, it means I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But that's not his statement. That's an Official Note. Surely that's an interpretation by this person who wrote this note, this Official Note, this Zeljko Vukovic. It's not the witness's statement, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this observation, Your Honour. I just said to the witness that this is the contents of his interview that he had with the police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And I want to ask him: Did he talk indeed to an officer at the police station?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: What do you want to know, the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You seem to be tired.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: No, you seem to be tired. You mentioned that I came on the 10th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we please have order in court. Witness, when I'm talking to the counsel, give us a chance to finish and I'm say to him he may continue, and then you can start talking to him. Your question, Mr. Milovancevic, you're saying that -- you read the statement and you're asking him now, did he give this statement in the police administration in 1992, and I'm saying to you this is not his statement. This is an Official Note by this person who signed that. When you say to him, "Did you give this statement," as you say here on the record, and he says yes to that, we are obviously misleading, both him and the Court. Now, you know as an officer of the Court that that's not his statement. That's an Official Note. Whatever interpretation that official put into what took place on that day, this witness will not know. You alleged that he made six different statements to the OTP. I'm still aware of three that you have been referring to. This Official Note is the fourth. I haven't seen the other three statements that you say he made to the OTP. Now, you have been confronting him with versions from the three statements. I have no problem with that. But I do have a problem when you attribute an Official Note to him as his statement. Now, when you say "did you make this statement or not" and you want to say did he say that point, that's not what he said. That's what he said by the official. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic, if you have -- or you can answer to what I have been saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were abundantly clear, Your Honour. Thank you. I will continue my questioning in such a way to solicit answers that could shed light on what exactly happened with this Official Note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I have before you, as do you, a certain Official Note. It says it was drawn up on the 1st of April, 1992, at the police administration of Sisak in connection with an interview conducted with you. It is written in the first paragraph. In the third paragraph it says: "Josip Josipovic has stated the following during this interview," and then follows a record of what you stated. My question is: Did you go to the police administration of Sisak, to the section for economic crimes, and did you have an interview there?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's just understand that what follows is what the official claims the witness said. It's not what the witness said. It's what the official claims the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2 of this Official Note, the officer who compiled this record, so this is an Official Note drawn up by an official of the police administration of Sisak, and it reads: "The interview was conducted at the Sisak police administration with a view to re-establishing employment in the police administration of Sisak and reinstating a residency in Dubica." Is that what the interview was about?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: When I came back from captivity, it was proven that I had not joined the Chetniks or Serb paramilitaries as some people had thought. I was not with Serb units. I was in captivity. That was the main purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to this officer who conducted this interview about the circumstances of your captivity in Dubica? Is that what you talked about?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On page 2 of this Official Note, the officer wrote down the following text which, according to this Official Note, should be a reflection of the interview he had with you, and I am going to put to you just a little passage from the second page of the B/C/S language you understand. In paragraphs 3 and 4 it reads: "The official or the officer recorded the following," after talking to you: "Momcilo Kovacevic is the commander and Stevo Radjun is the deputy. The area is under the control of local Chetniks who have a conflict with Martic's men. Local Chetniks are responsible for crimes committed against civilians, lootings, torchings and similar things, whereas the military police is trying to restore order and discipline." Another paragraph: "When in November 1991 Mile Martic came to inspect the area, he was in Zivaja but he didn't dare go to Dubica. Later on, military police managed to regain control. In the meantime, there had been several changes of authority." I just read out the text that the officer wrote down as a result of talking to you. That means based on the information you provided to that officer regarding your stay in Dubica. My question now is: This text regarding Momcilo Kovacevic and Stevo Radjun and their relationship with Milan Martic, is that a faithful reflection of what you said?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: You're really beginning to suffocate me or stifle me here. Perhaps we could have a short break. I think I need a rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How long of a rest do you need?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No translation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we have interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Five or 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: All right. If it's going to be 15 minutes, maybe it might just be the correct time to retire for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I have understood the witness correctly, he needs a short break of about 15 minutes, but that would bring us to the end of this session, so perhaps it would be best to finish by 7.00. I'm drawing to the end of my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not a problem. If we will end at 7.00, I can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I have another couple of questions for you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I can finish that then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll go up to 7.00. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: It's a brief question. What I've just read out to you, the contents of the Official Note, do the contents of the Official Note correspond to what you said to the police in 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, how am I to know whether it corresponds to what I said to the police in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I have a few more very brief questions. You gave your first statement to the Prosecution in the year 2000; is that correct? Can you remember that, although it was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the year or the date. I can't remember when I gave my first statement to the Prosecution. I can't remember when I first saw the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And one more question. Do you remember how it came to pass that you gave the Prosecution supplementary statements? Did you contact them yourself, or did they contact you in order to conduct another interview with you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They wanted an additional interview with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In those additional interviews, they put questions to you and you answered them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I answered their questions, if I was able to, and I provided them information I hadn't provided them with the first time I saw them. I didn't think it was that interesting nor did I think that it had any particular purpose or basis. I quite simply wanted to be done with it as soon as possible, and I didn't want to have to remember all of these events. I didn't think I had to say too much. As to whether there was anything of importance or not, I don't know. But in any event, at the time, The Hague Tribunal was interested in certain things and they wanted a supplementary statement. They wanted some additional explanations of certain events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I have no further questions for you. This concludes my cross-examination. Thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have now concluded my cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. It may very well be a convenient time. I don't think there is any purpose starting any re-examination at this point in time, Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I agree that we should continue tomorrow because it is clear the witness is tired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. And tomorrow we -- once again, I remind the parties we start at 10.00. This is in Courtroom I. Court adjourned until tomorrow at 10.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 7th day of April, 2006, at 10.00 a.m. 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.56 p.m.,
